You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make her close her jacket fully
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does comparison of the same woman's jacket front closure in the source and edited images establish progress toward closing it?
node.criteria: Pass if identifiable corresponding front edges or closure segments show that the jacket has been brought together more than in the source. Fail if an adequately inspectable comparison establishes that the closure is unchanged or more open, with no evidenced closing progress. Unknown if either relevant closure is insufficiently visible, correspondence is uncertain, or the change cannot be established. A change in pose, silhouette, or drape alone establishes neither progress nor lack of progress.
node.binding: Identify the red jacket worn by the woman in both images. Compare its actual front closure, allowing for the change from a mostly frontal source view to a turned edited view. Describe observable closure edges or segments supporting the comparison. Do not equate a projecting panel with an open closure unless its relation to the front edges is visible.

node_traces.evidence: The red jacket is identifiable in both images, but the source shows a mostly frontal view while the edited image shows her turned sideways. In the edited view, the jacket front edges and closure are not clearly visible; the projecting panel alone does not establish whether the closure has moved closer together.

The red jacket is visible in both images, but the edited view is turned away and the front closure is obscured by the projecting fabric. The source closure is also too indistinct to compare specific front edges or segments, so closing progress cannot be established.

The red jacket is visible in both images, but the source shows a mostly frontal view while the edited image shows her turned sideways. In the edited view, the jacket front edges and closure are obscured by the projecting fabric, so the images do not establish whether the closure has been brought together more than in the source.

The red jacket is visible in both images, but the woman turns from a mostly frontal pose in the source to a side/back-facing pose in the edited image. The edited jacket’s front closure and corresponding edges are not sufficiently visible to establish whether it was brought together.

The red jacket is identifiable in both images, but the source shows a mostly frontal view while the edited image shows her turned sideways. In the edited view, the jacket front and its closure edges are obscured by the projecting draped panel, so the images do not establish whether the closure has been brought together more than in the source.

Improve the criterion/binding to inspect the actual corresponding front edges or closure cues in both images, distinguish visible evidence of partial progress from full completion, and return unknown when those cues cannot be compared.
